routes.description: Establish a historically usable body of early testimony concerning Jesus' postmortem appearances and bodily resurrection, then show that an intentional divine resurrection explains that evidence more adequately than the proposed natural mechanisms under a defensible method of historical comparison.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the early testimony warrants the relevant appearance and bodily-resurrection claims, the resurrection hypothesis supplies the strongest unified explanation of them, and objections based on hallucination, source unreliability, missing-body alternatives, and antecedent improbability do not defeat that inference.

motionBridge.description: Connect the historically warranted appearance and bodily-resurrection evidence to the conclusion that Jesus rose and that this hypothesis better explains the testimony than naturalistic alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Establish that sufficiently early and historically usable sources report individual and group experiences interpreted as appearances of the risen Jesus and as bodily resurrection.
Show that hallucination, visionary contagion, disappearance, fabrication, and related natural proposals do not jointly match the evidence as well as the resurrection hypothesis.

Justify evaluating competing hypotheses through explanatory scope, power, ad hocness, and plausibility while handling disputed prior probabilities without excluding purposive divine action in advance.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how physical-body considerations, possible grave investigation, and the early proclaimers' sincere commitment constrain disappearance and fabrication accounts.
Defend the historical usability of the Gospel narrative core despite genre conventions, literary development, and discrepancies in peripheral details.

routes.description: Show that the surviving early testimony is sparse, culturally mediated, and compatible with ordinary processes such as visions, social reinforcement, disappearance, and narrative development, while arguing that its evidential force is insufficient to overcome the resurrection hypothesis's weak antecedent support.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if one or more collectively credible natural processes adequately account for the reported testimony without requiring a uniquely reconstructed history, and if source limitations and prior-probability considerations prevent that testimony from making resurrection the better historical explanation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the availability and collective plausibility of natural mechanisms, together with evidential limitations, to rejection of resurrection as the better explanation of early Christian testimony.

centralBridges.description: Establish that religious visions, charismatic suggestion, cultural reinforcement, cognitive processes, and ordinary missing-body scenarios can generate the central reported beliefs and traditions.

Show that a hypothesis involving resurrection requires unusually strong evidence because it lacks established background precedent and depends on prior commitments about divine existence and intention.
Demonstrate that the early epistolary record lacks sufficient detail and that later narrative sources contain features that limit their ability to establish bodily encounters and an empty grave.
Justify historical rejection of resurrection when several collectively likely natural scenarios remain available even if the evidence does not identify one complete natural reconstruction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how sincere believers could infer bodily resurrection without verifying an empty grave or could assimilate contrary physical evidence through prior religious commitments.
Account for the restricted appearance pattern and exceptional conversions as features expected within a localized visionary movement rather than public divine disclosure.

sections.title: Historical Method, Reference Classes, and Prior Probability
sections.rationale: The governing comparison determines whether explanatory criteria may bracket disputed priors or whether resurrection's lack of established precedent imposes an extraordinary evidential threshold; that choice structures every later inference from the testimony.

sections.title: Pauline Testimony and the Bodily Character of Resurrection
sections.rationale: The early Pauline material supplies the principal evidential base for appearances and bodily-resurrection belief, while its chronology, detail, interpretation, and capacity to support physical encounters remain central points of dispute.

sections.title: Visionary, Psychological, and Social-Contagion Explanations
sections.rationale: Competing accounts of individual and group experiences bear directly on whether ordinary religious and social processes can explain the appearance traditions or whether their phenomenology and distribution require a different causal account.

sections.title: Empty Grave, Investigation, and Proclaimer Sincerity
sections.rationale: Questions about disappearance, grave verification, bodily inference, and the costly sincerity of early proclaimers constrain both fabrication accounts and claims that vision-driven belief could develop independently of physical evidence.

sections.title: Historical Usability of the Gospel Narratives
sections.rationale: The status of Gospel detail affects whether empty-tomb and embodied-appearance narratives can supplement the sparse epistolary record, requiring attention to genre, embellishment, literary construction, external support, and contradictions.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Historical hypotheses should be compared by explanatory scope, explanatory power, avoidance of ad hoc assumptions, and plausibility rather than by subjective Bayesian priors.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted affirmative opening statement and explicit first-person framing identify Licona as the speaker.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the affirmative's governing method for comparing historical explanations and therefore has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly supplies a usable four-criterion framework central to the affirmative route.

precisionFindings.rationale: The four criteria and comparative task are recoverable, though the dismissal of subjective priors leaves a bounded methodological qualification implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The criteria are appropriate comparative tools, but the source excerpt does not fully warrant displacing rather than supplementing prior-probability analysis.

charity.alternative: Bayesian priors can complement explanatory criteria rather than merely express subjective preference.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not show that all defensible prior estimates are subjective or dispensable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative framework is coherent, but the bridge from useful explanatory criteria to rejecting Bayesian priors remains materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies recognized criteria but offers little defense here for their sufficiency or for excluding informed prior probabilities.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central historical-method bridge and sits near the top of that tier's relevance band.

representationalCharity.rationale: The alternative is implicitly narrowed to subjective priors, omitting the strongest objective-background-probability formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly enumerates explanatory scope and presents four criteria for selecting the best explanation, while providing no developed treatment of priors.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Early Pauline material reports individual and group appearances and supports the conclusion that Jesus and future Christians were understood to rise bodily.
moves.attributionBasis: The affirmative opening continues without a speaker transition, using Licona's announced positive historical case.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the affirmative's early testimonial basis for individual and group appearances and bodily resurrection, with no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly establishes the principal evidential propositions needed by the affirmative route.

precisionFindings.rationale: The appearance and bodily-resurrection claims are clear, but reports, beliefs, and established historical facts are insufficiently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the reported beliefs facts overstates what the excerpt alone establishes about transformed corpses and group encounters.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from early teaching to bodily belief is usable, but the move compresses the bridge from reports and beliefs to actual encounters.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt asserts Pauline and disciple beliefs but does not document texts, independence, chronology, or verification of the reported groups.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central testimonial basis and is maximally relevant within the central tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The selected span advances a positive source claim without materially characterizing a live opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says Christians and Christ were raised bodily and mentions appearances to individuals and groups, while labeling these reports and beliefs as facts.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: The resurrection hypothesis explains the reported appearances with comprehensive scope and power, without improper ad hocness or exclusion by worldview assumptions.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona explicitly applies the previously introduced criteria and closes his uninterrupted affirmative opening statement.

response.rationale: This constructive move applies the affirmative's criteria to the resurrection hypothesis itself and therefore has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly advances the motion-level inference, although its comparative demonstration is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claimed scope and power are clear, but the move does not state the conditions under which divine action avoids ad hocness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The assertion that the hypothesis could not explain the data better exceeds the limited comparative support supplied in the span.

charity.alternative: A natural explanation may cover the same reports through several interacting mechanisms.
charity.decisiveQualification: Unified coverage alone does not establish plausibility or superiority over collectively available rivals.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Resurrection would entail appearances, but compatibility is treated too quickly as powerful explanation and comparative superiority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The source supplies confident application of criteria but no representative rival comparison or defended warrant against ad hocness.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly connects the evidence to resurrection as the best explanation and therefore contacts the motion bridge directly.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move declares comprehensive superiority without seriously presenting the strongest multi-mechanism natural alternative or its qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says resurrection accounts for all individual and group appearances without forcing the data, but provides no detailed rival comparison in the selected span.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Because resurrection lacks established background precedent, the claim that Jesus rose requires evidence comparable to other extraordinary and otherwise unsupported claims.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator has yielded to Carrier, and the first-person comparison explicitly addresses the sufficiency of Mike's evidence.

components.text: Whether explanatory comparison may proceed without a defensible treatment of antecedent probability.
Whether the resurrection hypothesis has enough support to warrant its claimed explanatory superiority.

response.rationale: The starship analogy directly contests bracketing priors and argues that absent background precedent raises the evidential demand on resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a full answer that explicitly contacts the decisive prior-probability premise and its consequence for evidential sufficiency.

precisionFindings.rationale: The threshold claim is recoverable, though extraordinary evidence remains undefined and the analogy's relevant similarities are implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Low precedent reasonably raises the evidential burden, but the analogy does not itself specify how much evidence is required.

charity.alternative: Resurrection is a purposive singular act, not a repeatable natural frequency claim like ordinary revivification.
charity.decisiveQualification: A singular intentional act still requires background support for the agent and intention, but its reference class is disputed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from absent precedent to a higher evidential threshold is coherent, with one bounded bridge concerning the analogy's force.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The lack-of-precedent point supports caution, but the starship analogy substitutes for a developed base-rate and likelihood comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central evidential-threshold bridge and strongly constrains the affirmative method.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move captures the antecedent-support problem but initially compresses the strongest intentional-action qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier compares resurrection to owning a starship, expressly citing the lack of supporting generalization and concluding that extraordinary evidence is required.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Paul's letters portray vision-prone early Christians and do not establish detailed bodily encounters, so their reported appearances are reasonably explained as religious hallucinations.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier explicitly turns from Licona's presentation to the epistles and repeatedly distinguishes his reading from Mike's.

components.text: Whether Paul's early material establishes bodily encounters rather than culturally familiar visionary experiences.
Whether hallucination provides a natural explanation for the reported appearance experiences.

response.rationale: The move directly disputes the bodily interpretation of Pauline evidence and supplies a religious-hallucination alternative for the appearances.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully contacts the decisive evidential interpretation, though the textual demonstration remains less detailed than the claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast is clear, but hallucinating, ecstatic experience, and every Pauline appearance are treated too interchangeably.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Vision-proneness makes a visionary reading plausible, but the excerpt does not establish that all reported experiences were hallucinations.

charity.alternative: Pauline resurrection language may imply transformed embodiment even if the appearance phenomenology is sparse.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bodily belief does not by itself establish detailed physical encounters or exclude visionary experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The natural explanation follows plausibly from vision-prone context and sparse detail, with a bounded gap from propensity to each event.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move invokes scientific studies and Pauline ecstatic practice but supplies no representative study details or close textual analysis.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central testimonial basis by disputing what the earliest source can establish.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly separates bodily doctrine from encounter detail, though it somewhat compresses the transformed-body reading.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes studies of religious experience and says the earliest Christians regularly hallucinated and entered ecstatic states when turning to Paul's epistles.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: The restricted pattern of appearances and Paul's exceptional conversion fit a localized visionary movement and cognitive dissonance better than a compassionate deity publicly revealing a saving resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier continues his uninterrupted opening, explicitly contrasting an ordinary natural movement with the proposed divine appearance.

components.text: Whether the reported distribution of appearances is more expected under compassionate divine disclosure than under a localized movement.
Whether friend, foe, individual, and group reports make the appearance distribution independently compelling.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges the divine hypothesis through the restricted distribution and contrasts it with expectations for a natural movement, but it does not analyze every reported category.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer contacting the decisive distributional challenge while leaving the detailed testimonial categories untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative distribution claim is clear, with the divine-compassion premise carrying an implicit theology-dependent qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Restricted disclosure is evidence under the stated compassion model, but divine purposes are not independently established.

charity.alternative: A deity could rationally choose limited witnesses whose testimony initiates broader disclosure.
charity.decisiveQualification: That purpose remains possible but needs independent support to offset the restricted pattern.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The likelihood comparison is intelligible, but it depends materially on an unsupported prediction about compassionate divine behavior.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The restricted pattern is identified, yet the cognitive-dissonance and divine-intention warrants are asserted rather than demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary appearance-distribution bridge and lies at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes intentional divine action only through a narrow compassion expectation and underdevelops alternative purposes.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts worldwide continuing appearance with one small group and one outsider in one place and time, then invokes a natural movement.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: A missing body becomes substantially more significant when joined to prior resurrection predictions, reputed miracles, and sincere appearance reports involving friends, foes, individuals, and groups.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona frames the example, develops the Koresh comparison, and ends by explicitly asking Carrier whether the added context changes the inference.

components.text: Whether a missing body remains evidentially ordinary once resurrection-specific contextual evidence is added.
Whether sincere individual and group appearance reports add evidence beyond a bare disappearance.

response.rationale: The cumulative hypothetical answers the bare-base-rate objection by adding predictions, miracles, and varied sincere reports, while not independently establishing those additions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the decisive evidential-threshold demand and gives a substantially complete cumulative answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative claim is clear, but the status of predictions, miracles, sincerity, and missing-body evidence shifts between assumed and established.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The added facts would increase significance, but the move does not establish their reliability or comparative likelihood here.

charity.alternative: A missing body can remain ordinary if each added contextual claim is weak, dependent, or naturally explicable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cumulative force depends on the reliability and conditional independence of the added claims.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative-evidence inference is coherent, with one material bridge concerning whether the stipulated contextual claims are warranted.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Koresh-style hypothetical illustrates relevance but does not document the resurrection predictions, miracles, grave, or report independence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary empty-grave and sincerity bridge and is highly relevant within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move improves on a bare disappearance comparison but does not fully address dependence and reliability qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona contrasts an ordinary missing corpse with a context containing predictions, miracles, and sincere reports from friends, foes, individuals, and groups.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: A divine resurrection is an intentional act by a free agent and therefore belongs in a distinct reference class rather than the frequency class of naturally dead bodies.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly rejects Carrier's prior-probability treatment and articulates Licona's theistic free-agent reference-class argument.

components.text: Whether natural frequencies of dead bodies determine the prior probability of a purposive supernatural resurrection.

response.rationale: The move directly contests Carrier's natural reference class by classifying resurrection as a purposeful free-agent act, though it does not eliminate agent-and-intention priors.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive reference-class premise and offers a clear competing classification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The intentional-act distinction is clear, while its consequence for prior probability remains a bounded implicit qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker appropriately says probably and in my opinion, but uniqueness alone does not make the prior inscrutable or favorable.

charity.alternative: Intentional acts still admit priors based on evidence for the agent, motives, capacities, and comparable behavior.
charity.decisiveQualification: A unique event resists simple frequency counting without escaping probabilistic assessment altogether.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The category distinction is coherent, but the inference from purposive uniqueness to a reference class all by itself is underjustified.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies conceptual classification rather than evidence establishing a deity's existence, capability, or resurrection intention.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con side's central evidential-threshold bridge and is strongly relevant within the central tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The natural-death reference class is fairly challenged, but the strongest intentional-action Bayesian alternative remains unanswered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies resurrection as probably supernatural, performed by a deity for a specific purpose, and involving a deciding free agent.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Even a unique divine act depends on the prior probability that a god exists and intends that act, so uniqueness does not remove the resurrection's low prior.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier immediately answers Licona's reference-class claim and sustains the response through the extended exchange about inscrutability and prior probability.

components.text: Whether placing resurrection in a unique intentional-act class removes or neutralizes antecedent probability.
Whether prior probability can be bracketed as inscrutable during explanatory comparison.

response.rationale: Carrier expressly identifies the missing agent-and-intention priors and states the defeating consequence: uniqueness cannot yield a neutral probability or remove prior shrinkage.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly diagnoses the omitted probabilistic components and gives their consequence for the affirmative inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The agent-existence and particular-intention components are distinctly stated and applied to the claimed unique reference class.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move does not assign an exact prior and appropriately argues only that relevant prior components remain and may reduce probability.

charity.alternative: A unique intentional act may have an inscrutable rather than demonstrably tiny prior.
charity.decisiveQualification: Inscrutability does not justify assigning a neutral prior or omitting evidence about agent and intention.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The omitted-variable diagnosis is explicit and consistently shows why uniqueness alone cannot set or erase a prior.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The probabilistic warrant is strong conceptually, though no independent evidence quantifies the existence and intention components.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central evidential-threshold bridge at the highest level within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply directly engages the strongest uniqueness formulation and preserves its limited point while defeating the stronger consequence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier states that the probability must include God existing, planning, and executing the cause, and rejects treating uniqueness as a fifty-fifty chance.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: The appearance sequence can be explained as charismatic hallucinatory contagion in which Peter's private vision anchors and guides progressively larger groups into ecstatic visions.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier is directly asked what happened in the group appearances and develops a continuous, detailed causal reconstruction despite brief interlocutor challenges.

components.text: Whether natural mechanisms can causally explain the sequence of individual and group appearance reports.
Whether group reports independently require shared bodily encounters.

response.rationale: The move supplies a concrete causal sequence from a leader's private vision through suggestion-guided group ecstasy, directly answering the demand for a group mechanism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully and explicitly contacts the decisive natural-mechanism challenge with a developed causal reconstruction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed sequence is clear, but contagious hallucination, suggestion, and guided ecstatic visions are not carefully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The mechanism is presented as an expected sequence, although its application to these particular groups remains speculative.

charity.alternative: Group reports may represent multiple experiences or traditions rather than synchronized hallucinations requiring contagion.
charity.decisiveQualification: The sparse reports do not establish either synchronized perception or Carrier's reconstructed sequence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The leader-suggestion sequence is causally coherent, but several links from private vision to progressively larger groups remain assumed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Carrier references studies of contagion but provides no representative study details or evidence tying Peter and the groups to this sequence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central natural-mechanisms bridge and answers a principal explanatory challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers a serious alternative but speaks more specifically than the surviving report detail warrants.

moves.evidenceBasis: Carrier describes a charismatic leader whose private vision anchors, inspires, guides, and suggests experiences that become contagious among groups.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Altered-state explanations poorly fit the reported ordinary-consciousness features and do not plausibly generate belief in a bodily resurrection associated with an empty grave.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona cites comparative research on consciousness states and then states his own central objection concerning bodily resurrection and the grave.

components.text: Whether altered-state and contagion mechanisms fit the reported phenomenology of the resurrection appearances.
Whether visionary experiences plausibly produced bodily-resurrection belief.
Whether the appearance distribution is better explained by a localized visionary movement.

response.rationale: The ordinary-consciousness comparison and bodily-belief objection contact the phenomenology and belief-generation components, but do not answer the restricted-distribution argument.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong partial answer contacting the decisive mechanism and bodily-belief components while leaving distribution untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The OSC-versus-ASC comparison is identifiable, though which appearance reports supply six of ten characteristics is not specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move frames the research probabilistically, but sparse report detail limits confidence in classifying the experiences.

charity.alternative: Ecstatic or visionary causes can yield experiences later narrated with ordinary-consciousness and bodily features.
charity.decisiveQualification: Later report features may not transparently preserve the original phenomenology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A mismatch between reported features and altered states would count against the hypothesis, but source-to-phenomenology inference remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Comparative research and six claimed OSC qualities are mentioned, yet the qualities, reports, and classification procedure are not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central natural-mechanisms bridge and addresses its principal proposed group explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply engages altered states but underdevelops the strongest source-development qualification affecting its phenomenological inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona cites an OSC/ASC comparison, says at least six of ten ordinary-consciousness qualities appear in the reports, and adds bodily-resurrection and grave objections.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Vision-driven believers could infer bodily resurrection without checking a grave, or reinterpret contrary bodily evidence through assumptions, denial, and conspiratorial rationalization.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier directly rejects Licona's assumptions about what the disciples knew or checked and develops several mechanisms for sustaining their belief.

components.text: Whether believers needed an empty-grave verification before inferring bodily resurrection from visions.
Whether sincere appearance belief and bodily absence jointly make natural reinterpretation unlikely.

response.rationale: The move directly denies the assumed grave check and supplies denial, conspiracy, and rationalization mechanisms for sustaining bodily belief despite contrary evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully contacts the grave-verification premise and offers multiple explicit mechanisms addressing the cumulative objection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly presents alternative possibilities rather than claiming certainty about which specific rationalization occurred.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that believers could infer or preserve bodily belief without verification fits the illustrative support provided.

charity.decisiveQualification: The record does not establish that they knew, accessed, or actually checked the burial location.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary belief-without-body bridge and is maximally relevant within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply squarely addresses the strongest investigation assumption and identifies the decisive evidentiary absence without caricature.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: The sacrifices and persecution endured by Paul and leading disciples provide evidence that they sincerely believed their Christian proclamation.

components.text: Whether early proclaimers' belief can be dismissed as convenient rationalization rather than sincere conviction.
Whether costly commitment distinguishes truth from sincere visionary error.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts sincerity but leaves the decisive sincere-error mechanism substantially untouched.

charity.decisiveQualification: Sincerity defeats deliberate fabrication, not hallucination, misinterpretation, or social reinforcement.

moves.proposition: The earliest Christians probably believed they saw Jesus, although anthropological evidence means sincere proclamation cannot be treated as certain.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier explicitly states his probability judgment about lying, sincere belief, and what he infers from Paul's letters.

components.text: Whether costly sincere commitment establishes the truth of the proclaimed resurrection rather than merely belief.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply directly diagnoses the inferential limit of costly sincerity while preserving the well-supported narrower conclusion.

moves.proposition: The Gospels are historically unreliable because external evidence, redactional embellishment, literary borrowing, and contradictions indicate mythmaking rather than history.
